changes.title: The basic conditions
changes.location: Investigation II, V:243–251; internal page breaks not checked
changes.arabic_original_untouched: قال: المبحث الثاني. يشترط في الإمام أن يكون مكلفا حرا ذكرا عدلا، لأن غير العاقل من الصبي والمعتوه قاصر عن القيام بالأمور على ما ينبغي، والعبد مشغول بخدمة السيد لا يفرغ للأمر مستحقر في أعين الناس لا يهاب ولا يمتثل أمره، والنساء ناقصات عقل ودين ممنوعات عن الخروج إلى مشاهد الحكم ومعارك الحرب، والفاسق لا يصلح لأمر الدين ولا يوثق بأوامره ونواهيه، والظالم يختل به أمر الدين والدنيا، وكيف يصلح للولاية وما الوالي إلا لدفع شره؟ أليس بعجيب استرعاء الذئب؟ وأما الكافر فأمره ظاهر.
changes.revised_english: He says: Investigation Two. It is stipulated that the imam be subject to legal responsibility, free, male, and upright. A child or an intellectually impaired person who lacks rational capacity is incapable of discharging affairs as required. A slave is occupied with serving his master and has no leisure for the office; he is held in contempt by people, is not feared, and his commands are not obeyed. Women are deficient in intellect and religion and are forbidden to go out to the assemblies of government and the battlefields. A morally corrupt person is unsuited to religious affairs and cannot be trusted in his commands and prohibitions. An oppressor disrupts religious and worldly affairs: how could he be suited to govern, when a governor exists precisely to repel his evil? Is it not astonishing to entrust the flock to a wolf? As for an unbeliever, the matter is evident.
changes.editorial_note: Historical claims about gender, slavery, religious identity and eligibility must be attributed to this medieval author and not converted into editorial or contemporary prescriptions. The wolf/shepherd simile is rhetorical; taqlīf, freedom and 'adl are distinct conditions.

changes.title: Courage, independent judgement, and political competence
changes.arabic_original_untouched: وزاد الجمهور اشتراط أن يكون شجاعا لئلا يجبن عن إقامة الحدود ومقاومة الخصوم، مجتهدا في الأصول والفروع ليتمكن من القيام بأمر الدين، ذا رأي في تدبير الأمور لئلا يخبط في سياسة الجمهور. ولم يشترطها بعضهم لندرة اجتماعها في الشخص وجواز الاكتفاء فيها بالاستعانة من الغير، بأن يفوض أمر الحروب ومباشرة الخطوب إلى الشجعان ويستفتي المجتهدين في أمور الدين ويستشير أصحاب الآراء الصائبة في أمور الملك.
changes.revised_english: The majority add the stipulation that he be courageous, so that he does not shrink from implementing prescribed punishments and resisting opponents; qualified for independent reasoning in fundamental and derivative matters, so that he can discharge religious affairs; and possessed of judgement in administering affairs, so that he does not stumble blindly in governing the public. Some do not stipulate these qualifications, because they rarely coincide in one individual and because assistance from others can suffice: he may entrust warfare and the handling of dangerous situations to courageous men, seek rulings from qualified jurists on religious matters, and consult people of sound judgement on affairs of government.
changes.editorial_note: Reports disagreement over whether the three qualifications—courage, ijtihād in uṣūl and furūʿ, and administrative judgment—must coincide in one person. The dissent's precise substitute is delegated military command, consultation with mujtahids, and statecraft advice.

changes.title: The Qurashī condition: the author’s evidence
changes.arabic_original_untouched: واتفقت الأمة على اشتراط كونه قرشيا، أي من أولاد نضر بن كنانة، خلافا للخوارج وأكثر المعتزلة. لنا السنة والإجماع. أما السنة فقوله عليه الصلاة والسلام: الأئمة من قريش، وليس المراد إمامة الصلاة اتفاقا فتعينت الإمامة الكبرى، وقوله صلى الله عليه وسلم: الولاة من قريش ما أطاعوا الله واستقاموا لأمره، وقوله صلى الله عليه وسلم: قدموا قريشا ولا تقدموها. وأما الإجماع فهو أنه لما قال الأنصار يوم السقيفة: منا أمير ومنكم أمير، منعهم أبو بكر رضي الله تعالى عنه بعدم كونهم من قريش ولم ينكره عليه أحد من الصحابة فكان إجماعا.
changes.revised_english: The community agreed that he must be a Qurashī—that is, a descendant of al-Naḍr ibn Kināna—contrary to the Khārijites and most of the Muʿtazila. Our evidence is the Sunna and consensus. As for the Sunna, there is the Prophet’s saying, “The imams are from Quraysh.” By agreement, leadership of prayer is not intended, so the supreme imamate must be intended. There are also his sayings, “The rulers are from Quraysh so long as they obey God and remain steadfast in His command,” and, “Give Quraysh precedence and do not go ahead of them.” As for consensus, when the Helpers said at the Saqīfa, “A ruler from us and a ruler from you,” Abū Bakr prevented this on the ground that they were not from Quraysh. No Companion objected to him, and this therefore constituted consensus.
changes.editorial_note: The universal-consensus assertion is immediately limited by the author's acknowledgement that Khārijites and most Muʿtazilites dissent. The textual evidence is presented as prophetic reports and Saqīfa consensus; no independent hadith verification or modern endorsement. Emphasise leadership of prayer vs supreme imamate.

changes.title: Objections from transmission and reason
changes.arabic_original_untouched: احتج المخالف بالمنقول والمعقول. أما المنقول فقوله صلى الله عليه وسلم: أطيعوا ولو أمر عليكم عبد حبشي أجدع. وأجيب بأن ذلك في غير الإمام من الحكام جمعا بين الأدلة. وأما المعقول فهو أنه لا عبرة بالنسب في القيام بمصالح الملك والدين، بل للعلم والتقوى والبصيرة في الأمور والخبرة بالمصالح والقوة على الأهوال وما أشبه ذلك. وأجيب بالمنع، بل إن لشرف الأنساب وعظيم قدرها في النفوس أثرا تاما في اجتماع الآراء وتألف الأهواء وبذل الطاعة والانقياد وإظهار آثار الاعتقاد. ولهذا شاع في الأعصار أن يكون الملك والسياسة في قبيلة مخصوصة وأهل بيت معين حتى يرى الانتقال عنه من الخطوب العظيمة والاتفاقات العجيبة. ولا أليق بذلك من قريش الذين هم أشرف الناس، سيما وقد اقتصر عليهم ختم الرسالة وانتشرت منهم الشريعة الباقية إلى يوم القيامة.
changes.revised_english: The opponent appeals both to transmitted evidence and to reason. The transmitted evidence is the Prophet’s saying, “Obey, even if a mutilated Abyssinian slave is appointed over you.” The reply is that this concerns governing officials other than the imam, thereby reconciling the proofs. The rational argument is that lineage has no bearing on serving the interests of government and religion; what matters is knowledge, piety, insight into affairs, experience of public interests, strength in confronting dangers, and similar qualities. The reply denies this: noble lineage and its high standing in people’s minds have a decisive effect in uniting opinions, reconciling inclinations, securing obedience and submission, and bringing conviction into effect. Hence it has been common in successive ages for kingship and government to remain within a particular tribe and a designated household, so that their transfer elsewhere is regarded as a momentous event and an extraordinary occurrence. No group is more suited to this than Quraysh, the noblest of people, especially since the final messenger came exclusively from them and from them spread the Law that remains until the Day of Resurrection.
changes.editorial_note: The appeal to the Ethiopian-slave report and rational capacity argument are objections, not the author's position. The reply construes the report as applying to lesser governors; lineage is defended by psychological/social considerations. The reason's actual persuasive force remains an argumentative claim, not verified political science.

changes.title: Necessity and the exercise of government
changes.arabic_original_untouched: وأما إذا لم يوجد من قريش من يصلح لذلك أو لم يقتدر على نصبه لاستيلاء أهل الباطل وشوكة الظلمة وأرباب الضلالة فلا كلام في جواز تقلد القضاء وتنفيذ الأحكام وإقامة الحدود وجميع ما يتعلق بالإمام من كل ذي شوكة، كما إذا كان الإمام القرشي فاسقا أو جائرا أو جاهلا فضلا أن يكون مجتهدا. وبالجملة مبنى ما ذكر في باب الإمامة على الاختيار والاقتدار، وأما عند العجز والاضطرار واستيلاء الظلمة والكفار والفجار وتسلط الجبابرة الأشرار فقد صارت الرئاسة الدنيوية تغلبية وبنيت عليها الأحكام الدينية المنوطة بالإمام ضرورة، ولم يعبأ بعدم العلم والعدالة وسائر الشرائط. والضرورات تبيح المحظورات، وإلى الله المشتكى في النائبات وهو المرتجى لكشف الملمات.
changes.revised_english: But if no suitable person from Quraysh can be found, or if appointing him is beyond one’s power because those in falsehood have seized control and oppressors and people of error possess effective force, there is no question that anyone possessing effective power may assume judgeship, enforce rulings, implement prescribed punishments, and undertake all matters entrusted to the imam. The same applies when the Qurashī imam is morally corrupt, unjust, or ignorant, rather than being qualified for independent juristic reasoning. In sum, the discussions in the chapter on the imamate presuppose choice and ability. Where there is inability and necessity, where oppressors, unbelievers, and the wicked have taken control and evil tyrants dominate, worldly leadership has become a matter of predominance by force. The religious rulings dependent upon the imam are then attached to that leadership out of necessity, without regard to the absence of knowledge, uprightness, and the other qualifications. Necessities render prohibited things permissible. To God is complaint addressed in calamities, and in Him lies the hope of their removal.
changes.editorial_note: Crucial tension: when ideal personal qualifications or legitimate designation are unavailable, the author permits juridical functions by the possessor of shawka (effective coercive capacity) through necessity. Distinguish validity under necessity from praise of coercive seizure and don't collapse the levels of obligation/permission.

changes.title: Additional conditions attributed to Shiʿi groups
changes.arabic_original_untouched: قال: واشترطت الشيعة أمورا، منها أن يكون هاشميا، أي من أولاد هاشم بن عبد مناف أبي عبد المطلب، وليس لهم في ذلك شبهة فضلا عن حجة، وإنما قصدهم نفي إمامة أبي بكر وعمر وعثمان رضي الله عنهم. ومنهم من اشترط كونه علويا نفيا لخلافة بني العباس، وكفى بإجماع المسلمين على إمامة الأئمة الثلاثة حجة عليهم. ومنها أن يكون عالما بكل الأمور وأن يكون مطلعا على المغيبات، وهذه جهالة تفرد بها بعضهم.
changes.revised_english: He says: the Shiʿa stipulate further conditions. One is that the imam be a Hāshimite, a descendant of Hāshim ibn ʿAbd Manāf, the father of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib. They have no semblance of proof for this, let alone a genuine demonstration; their only purpose is to negate the imamates of Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, and ʿUthmān. Some stipulate that he be an ʿAlid, in order to negate the Abbasid caliphate. The Muslims’ consensus concerning the imamates of the first three is sufficient evidence against them. Another condition is that he know all things and have access to unseen matters. This is an ignorance peculiar to some of them.
changes.editorial_note: A polemical attribution of ʿAbbāsid and first-three-caliph disputes to Shīʿī groups; report Taftāzānī's judgment rather than adopting his blanket attribution or treating diversity among such groups as one system.

changes.title: Must the imam be the most excellent person?
changes.arabic_original_untouched: ومنها أن يكون أفضل أهل زمانه، لأن قبح تقديم المفضول على الأفضل في إقامة قوانين الشريعة وحفظ حوزة الإسلام معلوم للعقلاء ولا ترجيح في تقديم المساوي. ونقل مثل ذلك عن الأشعري، حتى لا تنعقد إمامة المفضول مع وجود الأفضل، لأن الأفضل أقرب إلى انقياد الناس له واجتماع الآراء على متابعته، ولأن الإمامة خلافة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فيجب أن يطلب لها من له رتبة أعلى قياسا على النبوة.
changes.revised_english: Another condition is that he be the most excellent person of his age. Rational people recognise the wrongness of giving someone inferior precedence over one superior in establishing the ordinances of the Law and protecting Islam’s domain; nor is there a ground of preference for giving precedence to an equal. A similar position is reported from al-Ashʿarī: the imamate of the less excellent is not constituted while the more excellent exists. The more excellent is more likely to secure people’s submission and the agreement of their opinions in following him. Moreover, the imamate is succession to the Prophet, so the person of higher rank must be sought for it, by analogy with prophecy.
changes.editorial_note: The reported al-Ashʿarī position and the Shiʿi argument are distinct from Taftāzānī's reply. Afḍal = superiority/excellence, not necessarily the most competent administrator; this contrast governs the next lemma.
changes.review_status: bounded electronic Arabic-English review, no new page-image certification

changes.title: Personal excellence and suitability for office
changes.arabic_original_untouched: وأجيب بأن القبح بمعنى استحقاق تاركه الذم والعقاب عند الله ممنوع، وبمعنى عدم ملاءمته بمجاري العقول والعادات غير مفيد، مع أنه أيضا في حيز المنع، إذ ربما يكون المفضول أقدر على القيام بمصالح الدين والملك ونصبه أوفق لانتظام حال الرعية وأوثق في اندفاع الفتنة. وهذا بخلاف النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم، فإنه مبعوث من العليم الحكيم الذي يختار من يشاء من عباده لنبوته ويوحي إليه مصالح الملك والملة ويراه أهلا لتبليغ ما أوحي إليه بمشيئته، فيدل ذلك قطعا على أفضليته. وإليه الإشارة بقوله تعالى: أفمن يهدي إلى الحق أحق أن يتبع أم من لا يهدي إلا أن يهدى فما لكم كيف تحكمون.
changes.revised_english: The reply is that wrongness in the sense that one who omits the preferential choice deserves blame and punishment from God is not conceded. Wrongness in the sense of being inappropriate to rational judgement and ordinary practice does not establish the desired conclusion; even that is open to denial. Someone less excellent may be more capable of attending to religious and governmental interests, and his appointment may be more conducive to the orderly condition of the subjects and more reliable in averting discord. The case of a prophet is different: he is sent by the All-Knowing and All-Wise, who chooses whom He wills from His servants for prophecy, reveals to him the interests of government and religion, and judges him fit to convey what He has willed to reveal. This certainly indicates his superiority. God’s words point to this: “Is one who guides to the truth more worthy of being followed, or one who cannot find guidance unless he is guided? What is the matter with you? How do you judge?”
changes.editorial_note: Keep two senses of qubḥ apart: legally punishable wrongness and unsuitability to reason/custom. The functional suitability of the mafdūl may outweigh rank; prophet's epistemic authentication differs because appointment is divine.

changes.title: Three further arguments—and a limit on their force
changes.arabic_original_untouched: وقد يحتج بجواز تقديم المفضول بوجوه. الأول إجماع العلماء بعد الخلفاء الراشدين على انعقاد الإمامة لبعض القرشيين مع أن فيهم من هو أفضل منه. الثاني أن عمر رضي الله عنه جعل الإمامة شورى بين ستة من غير نكير عليه، مع أن فيهم عثمان وعليا وهما أفضل من غيرهم إجماعا، ولو وجب تعيين الأفضل لعينهما. الثالث أن الأفضلية أمر خفي قلما يطلع عليه أهل الحل والعقد وربما يقع فيه النزاع ويتشوش الأمر. وإذا أنصفت فتعيين الأفضل متعسر في أقل فرقة من فرق الفاضلين فكيف في قريش مع كثرتهم وتفرقهم في الأطراف؟ وأنت خبير بأن هذا وأمثاله على تقدير تمامه إنما يصلح للاحتجاج على أهل الحق دون الروافض، فإن الإمام عندهم منصوب من قبل الحق لا من قبل الخلق.
changes.revised_english: Several further arguments may be offered for the permissibility of preferring the less excellent. First, after the rightly guided caliphs, scholars agreed that the imamate was constituted for certain Qurashīs even though others among them were more excellent. Second, ʿUmar entrusted the imamate to consultation among six without anyone objecting, although they included ʿUthmān and ʿAlī, who were by consensus superior to the others. Had designation of the most excellent been obligatory, he would have designated those two. Third, superiority in merit is hidden and rarely fully known to those empowered to bind and loose; disagreement about it may arise and disorder result. In fairness, identifying the most excellent is difficult even in the smallest group of virtuous people—how much more so among Quraysh, with their numbers and dispersion across the regions! You know, however, that these arguments and the like, even if complete, are suitable for use against the people of truth, not against the Rāfiḍa: according to the latter, the imam is appointed by the Truth, not by created beings.
changes.editorial_note: The Arabic final clause expressly says the arguments, if cogent, are against ahl al-ḥaqq and not al-Rawāfiḍ, whose own view makes appointment divine. Do not silently invert this surprising direction; note the argument from ʿUmar's six-person council pertains to human election.

changes.title: Immunity from sin and error: who bears the burden of proof?
changes.arabic_original_untouched: قال: وأن يكون معصوما. من معظم الخلافيات مع الشيعة اشتراطهم أن يكون الإمام معصوما، وقد عرفت معنى العصمة وأنها لا تنافي القدرة على المعصية بل ربما يستلزمها. واحتج أصحابنا على عدم وجوب العصمة بالإجماع على إمامة أبي بكر وعمر وعثمان رضي الله عنهم، مع الإجماع على أنهم لم تجب عصمتهم وإن كانوا معصومين بمعنى أنهم منذ آمنوا كان لهم ملكة اجتناب المعاصي مع التمكن منها. وحاصل هذا دعوى الإجماع على عدم اشتراط العصمة في الإمام، وإلا فليس للإجماع على عدم وجوب عصمة الشخص كثير معنى. وقد يحتج كثير بأن العصمة مما لا سبيل للعباد إلى الاطلاع عليه فإيجاب نصب إمام معصوم يعود إلى تكليف ما ليس في الوسع. وفي انتهاض الوجهين على الشيعة نظر. والظاهر أنه لا حاجة إلى الدليل على عدم الاشتراط، وإنما يحتاج إليه في الاشتراط.
changes.revised_english: He says: “And that he be immune from sin and error.” One of the principal disagreements with the Shiʿa concerns their stipulation that the imam possess such immunity. You already know the meaning of ʿiṣma and that it does not exclude the ability to sin—indeed, it may presuppose that ability. Our scholars argue against requiring it by appealing to consensus on the imamates of Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, and ʿUthmān, together with consensus that their immunity was not required, even if they were protected in the sense that, from the time they believed, they possessed a settled disposition to avoid sins while remaining capable of them. This amounts to a claim of consensus that immunity is not a condition of the imamate; otherwise, “consensus that a particular person’s immunity is not required” has little meaning. Another argument frequently offered is that people have no access to knowledge of such immunity. Requiring them to appoint an immune imam therefore amounts to requiring what lies beyond their capacity. Whether either argument succeeds against the Shiʿa is questionable. The evident position is that no proof is needed for the absence of this condition; proof is needed to establish the condition.
changes.editorial_note: The author grants that ʿiṣma does not abolish ability to sin and criticises his own side's two proof attempts against the Shīʿa. He shifts the burden of proof to those imposing an extraordinary condition; preserve this critical nuance rather than presenting simple consensus as decisive.
changes.review_status: bounded electronic Arabic-English review, no new page-image certification

changes.title: First argument for immunity: analogy with prophecy
changes.arabic_original_untouched: وقد احتجوا بوجوه. الأول القياس على النبوة بجامع إقامة الشريعة وتنفيذ الأحكام وحماية حوزة الإسلام. ورد بأن النبي مبعوث من الله مقرون دعواه بالمعجزات الباهرة الدالة على عصمته من الكذب وسائر الأمور المخلة بمرتبة النبوة ومنصب الرسالة، ولا كذلك الإمام فإن نصبه مفوض إلى العباد الذين لا سبيل لهم إلى معرفة عصمته واستقامة سريرته فلا وجه لاشتراطها. وأيضا النبي يأتي بالشريعة التي لا علم للعباد بها إلا من جهته، فلو لم يكن معصوما عن الكذب في تبليغها والفسق في تعاطيها، وقد لزمنا امتثاله فيما أمر ونهى واعتقاد إباحة ما جرى عليه ومضى، لكانت المعجزة التي أقامها الله تعالى لصحة الرسالة والهدى وانتظام أمر الدين والدنيا مفضية إلى الضلالة والردى واختلال حال العاجلة والعقبى.
changes.revised_english: They offer several arguments. The first is analogy with prophecy, on the shared ground of establishing the Law, enforcing rulings, and protecting Islam’s domain. The reply is that a prophet is sent by God and his claim is accompanied by manifest miracles indicating his immunity from lying and from everything incompatible with the rank of prophecy and the office of messenger. The imam is not like this: his appointment is entrusted to people who have no way of knowing his immunity or the rectitude of his inner state, so there is no basis for making it a condition. Moreover, a prophet brings a Law which people know only through him. Were he not protected from lying in conveying it and from immoral conduct in practising it, while we were obliged to obey his commands and prohibitions and regard his conduct as permissible, the miracle established by God to authenticate the message, provide guidance, and order religious and worldly affairs would lead instead to error, ruin, and disorder in this life and the next.
changes.editorial_note: The analogical argument fails because prophetic verification involves mission/miracle and original access to revealed law, unlike appointment by human electors. The danger of a false prophet conveying law is a separate second reply.

changes.title: Second argument: obligatory obedience
changes.arabic_original_untouched: الثاني أن الإمام واجب الطاعة بالنص والإجماع، قال الله تعالى: أطيعوا الله وأطيعوا الرسول وأولي الأمر منكم. وكل واجب الطاعة واجب العصمة، وإلا لجاز أن يكذب في تقرير الأوامر والنواهي وينهى عن الطاعات ويأمر بالمعاصي، فيلزم وجوب اجتناب الطاعة وارتكاب العصيان، واللازم ظاهر البطلان. والجواب أن وجوب طاعته إنما هو فيما لا يخالف الشرع، بشهادة قوله تعالى: فإن تنازعتم في شيء فردوه إلى الله والرسول. ويكفي في عدم كذبه في بيان الأحكام العلم والعدالة والإسلام. وهذا ما يقال: إنما يجب عصمته لو كان وجوب طاعته بمجرد قوله، وأما إذا كان لكونه حكم الله ورسوله فيكفي العلم والعدالة، كالقاضي والوالي بالنسبة إلى الخلق والشاهد بالنسبة إلى الحاكم والمفتي بالنسبة إلى المقلد وأمثال ذلك. على أن الإجماع عند الشيعة إنما يكون حجة لاشتماله على قول المعصوم فإثبات العصمة به دور.
changes.revised_english: The second is that obedience to the imam is obligatory by explicit revelation and consensus. God says, “Obey God, obey the Messenger, and those vested with authority among you.” Whoever must be obeyed must possess immunity; otherwise he could lie when declaring commands and prohibitions, forbid acts of obedience, and command sins. Avoiding obedience and committing disobedience would then become obligatory—an obviously false consequence. The reply is that obedience to him is obligatory only where it does not conflict with the Law, as witnessed by God’s words, “If you disagree about anything, refer it to God and the Messenger.” Knowledge, uprightness, and Islam suffice as grounds for relying on his not lying in explaining rulings. This is the point of saying that immunity would be required if obedience were obligatory merely because he said something. Where obedience is obligatory because it is God’s and His Messenger’s ruling, knowledge and uprightness suffice—as with a judge or governor in relation to the people, a witness in relation to the judge, a mufti in relation to the person following his judgement, and similar cases. Furthermore, according to the Shiʿa, consensus is authoritative only because it includes the statement of an immune imam. Establishing immunity by consensus would therefore be circular.
changes.editorial_note: The unrestricted-command reading of Qurʾān 4:59 is challenged by the same verse's dispute-clause, so authority is obedience in lawful acts; ijmāʿ cannot prove a sinless imam under a theory defining its authority by already including one, owing to circularity.

changes.title: Third argument: the covenant does not extend to wrongdoers
changes.arabic_original_untouched: الثالث أن غير المعصوم ظالم لأن المعصية ظلم على النفس أو على الغير، ولا شيء من الظالم بأهل للإمامة لقوله تعالى: لا ينال عهدي الظالمين. والمراد عهد الإمامة بقرينة السباق وهو قوله تعالى: إني جاعلك للناس إماما قال ومن ذريتي. والجواب أن غير المعصوم، أي من ليس له ملكة العصمة، لا يلزم أن يكون عاصيا بالفعل فضلا أن يكون ظالما، فإن المعصية أعم من الظلم وليس كل عاص ظالما على الإطلاق. ولو سلم فدلالة الآية على صدق الكبرى لا تتم لجواز أن يكون المراد عهد النبوة والرسالة على ما هو رأي أكثر المفسرين. نعم لا يبعد إثباته بالإجماع وفيه ما مر.
changes.revised_english: The third is that anyone who lacks immunity is a wrongdoer, since sin wrongs oneself or someone else; and no wrongdoer is eligible for the imamate, because God says, “My covenant does not extend to the wrongdoers.” The covenant of imamate is intended, as indicated by the preceding words, “I shall make you an imam for the people.” Abraham said, “And from my descendants?” The reply is that someone without immunity—that is, without the disposition of ʿiṣma—need not actually be a sinner, let alone a wrongdoer. Sin is broader than wrongdoing, and not every sinner is unqualifiedly called a wrongdoer. Even if this is conceded, the verse does not fully establish the major premise: the covenant of prophecy and messengership may be intended, as most commentators hold. It would not be implausible to establish the premise by consensus, but that encounters the difficulty already mentioned.
changes.editorial_note: Logical issue: non-possession of an ʿiṣma-disposition does not imply actually committing sin, let alone being classified absolutely as ẓālim. Even granting this, the divine 'covenant' might refer to prophecy rather than political imamate. Two independent rebuttal levels must remain clear.

changes.title: Fourth argument: an infinite regress of supervisors
changes.arabic_original_untouched: الرابع أن الأمة إنما يحتاجون إلى الإمام لجواز الخطأ عليهم في العلم والعمل ولذلك يكون الإمام لطفا لهم، فلو جاز الخطأ على الإمام لوجب له إمام آخر ويتسلسل. وشبه ذلك بانتهاء سلسلة الممكنات إلى الواجب لئلا يلزم التسلسل. والجواب أن وجوب الإمام شرعي بمعنى أنه أوجب علينا نصبه لا عقلي مبني على جواز الخطأ على الأمة كما زعمتم، لأن في الشريعة القائمة إلى القيامة غنية عنه لولا إيجاب الشارع. والضرر المظنون من عدمه يندفع بعلمه واجتهاده وظاهر عدالته وحسن اعتقاده وإن لم يكن معصوما. ألا يرى أن الخطأ جائز على المعصوم أيضا لما عرفت من أن العصمة لا تزيل المحنة؟ وإن لم يندفع بذلك فكفى بخبر الأمم وعلماء الشرع مانعا دافعا.
changes.revised_english: The fourth argument is that the community needs an imam because its members may err in knowledge and action; hence the imam is an assistance (*luṭf*) to it. If he, too, may err, he would need another imam, and an infinite regress would follow. This is compared to terminating the sequence of contingent beings at the Necessary Being to avoid regress. The reply is that the obligation to appoint an imam is a revealed obligation: the Lawgiver has required us to appoint one. It is not a rational obligation founded upon the community's susceptibility to error, as the opponents claim; absent the Lawgiver's command, the Law that endures until the Resurrection would suffice. The probable harm occasioned by an imam's absence may be averted by his knowledge, independent judgement, apparent uprightness and sound conviction, even without his being infallible. For even someone endowed with protection from sin remains *capable* of error—protection does not abolish moral testing, as was explained. And even if those qualifications do not avert the harm, the experience of nations and the scholars of the Law can provide restraint and protection.
changes.editorial_note: Problematic modal wording: يجوز الخطأ على المعصوم does not say a protected person actually errs; ʿiṣma leaves the capacity/testability for wrongdoing and must not be rendered as denial of the protection. The first rebuttal denies the rational error-correction regress; the alternative relies on revealed law, juristic competence, communal scholars.

changes.title: Fifth argument: preservation of the Law
changes.arabic_original_untouched: الخامس أنه حافظ للشريعة، فلو جاز الخطأ عليه لكان ناقضا لها لا حافظا فيعود على موضوعه بالنقض. والجواب أنه ليس حافظا لها بذاته بل بالكتاب والسنة وإجماع الأمة واجتهاده الصحيح، فإن أخطأ في اجتهاده أو ارتكب معصية فالمجتهدون يردون والآمرون بالمعروف يصدون. وإن لم يفعلوا أيضا فلا نقض للشريعة القويمة ولا نقض على الطريقة المستقيمة.
changes.revised_english: The fifth is that the imam preserves the Law. If error were possible for him, he would undermine it rather than preserve it, contradicting the purpose of his own institution. The reply is that he does not preserve it by himself, but through the Book, the Sunna, the community’s consensus, and his sound independent reasoning. If he errs in his reasoning or commits a sin, qualified jurists refute him and those commanding right restrain him. Even if they fail to do so, the upright Law is not thereby annulled, nor is the straight path overturned.
changes.editorial_note: The argument assumes that imperfect custodianship would negate the Law itself. The reply identifies preservation with Book, Sunna, communal consensus, legal reasoning and correction by scholars rather than infallibility of an individual.

changes.title: Sixth argument: can obedience coexist with correction?
changes.arabic_original_untouched: السادس أنه لو أقدم على المعصية فإما أن يجب الإنكار عليه وهو مضاد لوجوب إطاعته الثابت بقوله تعالى: أطيعوا الله وأطيعوا الرسول وأولي الأمر منكم، فيلزم اجتماع الضدين، وإما أن لا يجب وهو خلاف النص والإجماع. والجواب أن وجوب الطاعة إنما هو فيما لا يخالف الشرع، وأما فيما يخالفه فالرد والإنكار وإن لم يتيسر فسكوت عن اضطرار.
changes.revised_english: The sixth is that if he commits a sin, either objection to him is obligatory or it is not. If it is obligatory, it conflicts with the obligation to obey him established by God’s words, “Obey God, obey the Messenger, and those vested with authority among you,” so two contraries would coincide. If it is not obligatory, this contradicts revelation and consensus. The reply is that obedience is obligatory only in matters that do not contravene the Law. In matters that do, rejection and objection are required; where these are not possible, silence results from necessity.
changes.editorial_note: Lawful orders and unlawful acts form different scopes, so obeying and objecting are not contradictory; 'silence from necessity' is a concession about inability to act, not blanket legal indifference.

changes.title: Seventh argument: transmitting the Law
changes.arabic_original_untouched: السابع أنه لا بد للشريعة من ناقل ولا يوجد في كل حكم حكم أهل التواتر معنا إلى انقراض العصر، فلم يبق إلا أن يكون إماما معصوما عن الخطأ. والجواب أن الظن كاف في البعض فينقل بطريق الآحاد من الثقات، وأما القطعي فإلى أهل التواتر أو جميع الأمة وهم أهل عصمة عن الخطأ فلا حاجة إلى معصوم بالمعنى الذي قصدتم. وليت شعري بأي طريق نقلت الشريعة إلى الشيعة من الإمام الذي لا يوجد منه إلا الاسم؟
changes.revised_english: The seventh is that the Law must have a transmitter, whereas in every individual ruling we do not have transmitters sufficient for mass transmission remaining with us until the age ends. The transmitter must therefore be an imam immune from error. The reply is that probable knowledge suffices in some matters, which are transmitted by trustworthy individuals through reports below the level of mass transmission. Matters requiring certainty are entrusted to mass transmitters or to the whole community, which is protected from error. There is therefore no need for an immune individual in the sense you intend. Would that I knew by what route the Law has reached the Shiʿa from an imam of whom nothing is present but the name!
changes.editorial_note: Distinguish āḥād reliable reports yielding zann from tawātur/entire-community evidence yielding qatʿ. The final polemical question about an absent imam is the author's, not an independent historical demonstration.

changes.title: Extraordinary qualifications attributed to extremists
changes.location: End of Investigation II; Investigation III begins at V:252
changes.arabic_original_untouched: قال: وأما اشتراط. قد اشترط الغلاة من الروافض أن يكون الإمام صاحب معجزة عالما بالغيوب وبجميع اللغات وبجميع الحرف والصناعات وبطبائع الأغذية والأدوية وبعجائب البر والبحر والسماء والأرض. وهذه خرافات مفضية إلى نفي الإمام ورفض الشريعة والأحكام.
changes.revised_english: He says: “As for the stipulation …” The extremists among the Rāfiḍa have stipulated that the imam work miracles, know unseen matters, all languages, all crafts and trades, the natures of foods and medicines, and the wonders of land, sea, heaven, and earth. These are fables leading to the denial of the imam and the abandonment of the Law and its rulings.
changes.editorial_note: The stated conditions of miracle, omniscience, languages and natural lore are attributed polemically to unnamed extremists, not all Shīʿī traditions. The concluding 'khurāfāt' is the author's judgement and should be marked as such.
